newsitem.title: PUERTO RICO: Nineteen dead, 63 hurt in Puerto Rico blast.
newsitem.headline: Nineteen dead, 63 hurt in Puerto Rico blast.

text.p: Victims buried in rubble cried out for help on Thursday after a shopping centre and apartment building was demolished in an apparent natural gas explosion that killed 19 people and injured at least 63.
More than six hours after the early morning blast in a shoe store, police said they could hear a man and a woman calling out, "Estamos aqui, estamos aqui!" -- "We are here, we are here!"

Work crews were trying frantically to reach them. The blast destroyed the six-floor building in the busy Rio Piedras commercial district in San Juan, burying the victims under twisted metal beams and broken concrete. There were five floors of apartments over the shops in the building.
"We are still concentrating on removing the rubble to get more people out," Juan Carlos Molina, spokesman for Gov. Pedro Rosello, said.

A church across the street served as a makeshift morgue. Health officials said many injuries were severe. "We've got four or five patients on respirators, several others with severe burns and many more patients on the way," Puerto Rico Health Secretary Carmen Feliciano said at a nearby hospital.
Rescue workers commandeered ambulances from surrounding communities and issued a plea for blood donations, especially O-negative blood.

Molina said a gas leak was believed to have caused the blast. "The authorities are fairly certain that the explosion was due to a gas leak. Some personnel from San Juan Gas were seen in the vicinity working on a gas pipe, then a little afterward was the explosion. It was a rather large explosion."

The force of the blast threw several parked cars onto their sides and flipped over a large San Juan Gas Company truck. The building that housed the Humberto Vidal shoe store was reduced to an empty shell. Neighbouring buildings were heavily damaged and debris covered a one-block area.
A Catholic elementary school, La Milagrosa, was damaged by the explosion but no students were hurt, Molina said. Nuns at the school rushed to comfort the victims.
The blast occurred during the morning rush hour, near a crowded plaza that served as an informal terminal for commuter vans and a gathering place for elderly domino players.
Stores up to 220 yards (200 metres) away had their glass shattered by the explosion.
